title: Bitcoin Slides Below $64,000 as Fed Hike Fears Hammer Crypto
content: Bitcoin fell to around $63,900 by Saturday, down about 5% over 24 hours and nearly 50% below its record high near $126,000, as mounting bets on a December US rate hike and a renewed sell-off in technology shares drained risk appetite. Ether fared worse, sliding to roughly $1,930 — down about 13% on the week — before slipping towards $1,700 in later trade, while roughly $1.5bn of leveraged positions were liquidated on Thursday alone. Spot bitcoin ETFs have bled about $2bn over three weeks, and the broad crypto market has shed an estimated $550bn in value since October.
summary: Bitcoin dropped below $64,000 and Ether neared $1,700 as December Fed rate-hike bets and a tech sell-off drove a broad crypto rout.
context:
• Digital assets have traded in close sympathy with high-beta technology stocks through 2026, amplifying losses whenever risk appetite sours.

• Spot bitcoin and ether ETFs have become a key marginal source of demand, so sustained outflows now weigh directly on prices.

• A hawkish repricing of Fed policy — with markets now expecting rate rises rather than cuts — has lifted real yields and sapped appetite for non-yielding assets.
happened:
• Bitcoin traded near $63,900 on Saturday, down about 5% in 24 hours, while Ether fell to roughly $1,930 and later slipped towards $1,700.

• Around $1.5bn of leveraged crypto positions were liquidated on Thursday as the sell-off accelerated.

• US spot bitcoin ETFs have recorded roughly $2bn of net outflows over three weeks, and the total crypto market has lost an estimated $550bn since October.
implications:
• Persistent ETF redemptions would remove a pillar of demand and leave the market more exposed to forced, leveraged selling.

• A firmer Fed path and higher real yields could keep pressure on speculative assets into the December meeting.

• A decisive break below recent support risks triggering a further cascade of liquidations across leveraged positions.
importance:
• Bitcoin has become a real-time barometer of broad risk appetite, so its slide signals caution spreading across markets.

• ETF flows offer a transparent read on institutional positioning that traders now watch closely.

• The rout underlines how tightly digital assets are tied to the fate of the AI-driven risk trade and the rates outlook.

title: Markets Brace for a December Fed Hike as Inflation Runs Hot
content: Investors swung to pricing a US interest-rate increase at the Federal Reserve's 8–9 December meeting after October data showed inflation reaccelerating, a sharp reversal from the rate cuts expected only weeks ago. Producer prices rose 6.5% over the year, the largest annual gain since 2022, while core consumer prices climbed 0.3% on the month, keeping alive the prospect of a larger half-point move. The CME FedWatch tool put the odds of a 50-basis-point December hike at about 11%, up from zero a week earlier, and several banks now forecast increases stretching into 2027.
summary: Hot October inflation data pushed markets to price a December Fed rate hike, with some betting on a larger half-point move.
context:
• The Fed has already lifted its policy rate once in 2026, to 3.75%–4.00% in September, as inflation proved stickier than expected.

• Markets spent much of the autumn positioning for rate cuts, so the hawkish turn has forced an abrupt repricing across asset classes.

• Governor Christopher Waller had flagged he could support a 50bp move if core CPI came in around 0.3% or higher — which October's reading did.
happened:
• October producer prices rose 6.5% year on year, the fastest since 2022, and core consumer prices increased 0.3% on the month, both at or above forecasts.

• Markets moved to price a quarter-point hike at the 8–9 December meeting, with a further increase expected in January.

• CME FedWatch showed roughly an 11% chance of a 50bp December hike, up from zero a week before, as Treasury yields climbed.
implications:
• A hiking Fed would tighten financial conditions further, pressuring richly valued equities and raising borrowing costs across the economy.

• Bank of America now expects increases at the next three meetings, implying a materially higher terminal rate than markets assumed in October.

• Any upside surprise in coming data could revive debate over a half-point move and sharpen cross-asset volatility.
importance:
• A pivot from cuts to hikes upends the central assumption underpinning this year's risk rally.

• Rate expectations anchor valuations across equities, credit, currencies and commodities, so the repricing reverberates everywhere.

• The episode leaves markets unusually sensitive to every inflation print into year-end.

title: Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO, Rattling the AI Trade
content: Nvidia said on Thursday that Jensen Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, an abrupt exit that wiped more than $600bn from the chipmaker's market value over the week. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO while the board, now chaired for the first time by former Synopsys chief Harvey Jones, searches for a permanent successor among internal and external candidates. Nvidia shares fell about 2% on Friday, dragging on US indices and sending a fresh jolt through AI-linked stocks worldwide.
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned with immediate effect, with CFO Colette Kress named interim chief, as more than $600bn was wiped off the company's value.
context:
• Nvidia sits at the centre of the global AI trade, so leadership there moves semiconductors, megacap tech and risk sentiment broadly.

• Huang had led the company for more than three decades and was widely seen as having no designated successor, heightening uncertainty.

• The exit lands just as investors were already questioning whether vast AI infrastructure spending will pay off.
happened:
• Nvidia disclosed in a securities filing on 12 November that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, with no reason given.

• CFO Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO while retaining her finance role, and former Synopsys chief Harvey Jones became the board's first chair.

• Nvidia shares dropped about 2% on Friday and lost more than $600bn in market value over the week.
implications:
• A prolonged search for a permanent CEO could keep an uncertainty discount on the shares and across the wider chip complex.

• Any perceived change in strategy or execution risks rippling through Nvidia's dense web of suppliers and AI customers.

• Clarity on succession and continuity of the product roadmap will be critical to stabilising sentiment.
importance:
• Nvidia's sheer index weight means its swings move the S&P 500 and Nasdaq directly.

• The leadership shock crystallises market anxiety about the durability of the AI boom.

• Next week's Nvidia earnings now carry added weight as investors seek reassurance on demand and direction.

title: Wall Street Notches Best Week Since August Despite Friday Wobble
content: The S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,561.67, down 0.4% on the day but up about 2.5% on the week — its first winning week since October and biggest weekly gain since August — as a rebound in battered shares offset a late tech sell-off. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.9% on Friday to 25,136.27 yet still rose roughly 2.3% over the week, snapping a four-week losing run, while the Dow added about 2% and the Russell 2000 gained 1.3%. Breadth was firm, with more than 60% of S&P 500 members higher on Friday even as Nvidia's slide weighed on the index.
summary: The S&P 500 rose about 2.5% on the week, its best since August, despite a Friday dip led by technology shares.
context:
• US equities had endured a bruising autumn sell-off driven by doubts over AI spending and stretched megacap valuations.

• Market leadership has been unusually narrow, so broadening participation is closely watched as a sign of health.

• The bounce came even as rate expectations turned more hawkish, underscoring resilient earnings optimism.
happened:
• The S&P 500 finished at 7,561.67 (-0.4%) on Friday but gained about 2.5% on the week; the Nasdaq rose 2.3% despite a 0.9% Friday drop.

• The Dow climbed roughly 2% on the week and the small-cap Russell 2000 added about 1.3%.

• More than 60% of S&P 500 stocks rose on Friday, with the equal-weighted index outperforming as Nvidia dragged on the cap-weighted benchmark.
implications:
• Firmer breadth would ease concerns that the rally rests on a handful of megacaps, but a hawkish Fed could cap further gains.

• Next week's Nvidia earnings loom as a key test of whether the AI trade can stabilise.

• Persistent two-way swings point to elevated volatility into year-end as rate and AI narratives collide.
importance:
• The first winning week since October offers tentative evidence that dip-buyers remain active after the autumn rout.

• Improving breadth is a constructive signal for the durability of any recovery.

• With the S&P still up around 11% in 2026, the stakes into year-end are high for performance-chasing investors.

title: Anthropic Lines Up Record Nasdaq Listing Into a Tech Sell-Off
content: Anthropic, the artificial-intelligence company behind the Claude models, is targeting a Nasdaq debut as soon as the week of 17 November under the ticker 'ANT', in what could rank as the largest initial public offering on record. Reports put the indicative range at $70–$78 a share and valuation estimates between roughly $1.4tn and $2tn, with the raise potentially exceeding $60bn — pricing into one of the sharpest AI-stock sell-offs of the year. The float has drawn scrutiny over its financing arrangements, including a reported commitment from Broadcom to lend up to $42bn via convertible notes to help fund Anthropic's chip leases.
summary: Anthropic is targeting a potentially record Nasdaq IPO under ticker 'ANT' at a valuation estimated between $1.4tn and $2tn, even as AI stocks sell off.
context:
• The listing would be the most prominent AI IPO yet and a major test of public-market appetite for the sector after a turbulent autumn.

• Anthropic filed confidentially in June and last raised privately at a reported valuation near $965bn, implying a steep mark-up.

• A reported $42bn Broadcom financing package covers roughly a third of Anthropic's $125.2bn, five-year commitment to lease tensor processing units.
happened:
• Reports indicate Anthropic is aiming to begin trading on Nasdaq around 19–20 November under the ticker 'ANT', at an indicative $70–$78 per share.

• Valuation estimates range from about $1.4tn to $2tn, with the offering potentially raising more than $60bn.

• Scrutiny has centred on the Broadcom convertible-note arrangement, which analysts have flagged as a form of circular financing.
implications:
• A strong debut would reopen the AI-IPO window and bolster sentiment; a weak one could deepen doubts about stretched sector valuations.

• The sheer scale of the raise could pull liquidity from other richly valued technology names.

• The circular-financing concerns may intensify debate over how AI infrastructure is being funded across the industry.
importance:
• At the mooted size, the listing would be a landmark event for equity markets and AI investment alike.

• Its reception will serve as a real-time referendum on investor conviction in the AI build-out.

• The deal spotlights the web of supplier-financing ties binding chipmakers and AI developers.

title: European Shares Hit Records, Cap Best Week Since June
content: The pan-European STOXX 600 edged up to a record close of 664.14 on Friday and gained about 2.4% on the week, its strongest showing since June, as robust corporate earnings and strength in insurers and oil majors offset a chip-led sell-off sparked by Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia. Germany's DAX rose roughly 3.6% on the week, the FTSE 100 climbed to a three-month high near 10,903 and France's CAC 40 also advanced. Third-quarter profits for STOXX 600 companies are tracking about 25% growth, the fastest in four years.
summary: The STOXX 600 closed at a record and rose about 2.4% on the week — its best since June — as strong earnings offset a Friday tech sell-off.
context:
• European equities have outpaced the S&P 500 in 2026, helped by cheaper valuations and a rotation away from US megacap tech.

• Financials, energy and defence have underpinned the regional rally, broadening leadership beyond technology.

• A resurgent earnings season has given investors fresh reason to add exposure despite global AI jitters.
happened:
• The STOXX 600 closed up 0.02% at a record 664.14 on Friday, taking its weekly gain to about 2.4%.

• The DAX rose roughly 3.6% on the week, the FTSE 100 hit a three-month high around 10,903, and the CAC 40 edged higher.

• Insurers and oil majors offset a Friday slide in chip stocks tied to Nvidia's leadership shock.
implications:
• Continued earnings strength could sustain Europe's outperformance if US tech remains volatile.

• A deepening global AI sell-off would nonetheless test the region's more cyclical, value-tilted indices.

• Record highs raise the bar for fresh catalysts to drive the next leg higher.
importance:
• Europe's leadership this year challenges the long-standing assumption of permanent US equity dominance.

• Broadening participation across sectors is a constructive signal for the rally's durability.

• The divergence offers global investors a diversification case away from concentrated US tech.

title: Nikkei Posts Strongest Week in Five Months Even as SoftBank Slides
content: Japan's Nikkei 225 closed Friday at 61,142.35, up 0.5% on the day and about 6.5% on the week — its best weekly performance in five months — as strong corporate earnings outweighed the gloom from Jensen Huang's resignation at Nvidia. SoftBank Group, the market's bellwether for AI exposure, bucked the trend to fall around 5% on Friday, the single biggest drag on the benchmark. An early tech-led rally faded late in the session as investors weighed yen weakness, rising Japanese government bond yields and fresh uncertainty over the global AI cycle.
summary: The Nikkei 225 rose about 6.5% on the week, its best in five months, though SoftBank fell around 5% on Friday after Nvidia's leadership shock.
context:
• The Nikkei has been among the world's best-performing major indices in 2026, powered by AI-linked and semiconductor names.

• SoftBank trades as a high-beta proxy for AI sentiment, so Nvidia news tends to move it sharply.

• Japanese markets are also contending with a weak yen and rising domestic bond yields that complicate the policy backdrop.
happened:
• The Nikkei 225 closed at 61,142.35 on Friday (+0.53%), up about 6.5% on the week.

• SoftBank Group fell around 5%, the biggest negative contributor, after Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia.

• An early rally faded as investors weighed yen softness, higher Japanese government bond yields and AI-sector uncertainty.
implications:
• Continued earnings momentum could underpin the Nikkei, but heavy AI exposure leaves it sensitive to Nvidia's fortunes.

• A weaker yen supports exporters yet raises the risk of official intervention and complicates the Bank of Japan's path.

• Rising government bond yields add a domestic headwind to richly valued chip shares.
importance:
• Japan's rally has been a standout in global equities, so its resilience matters for risk sentiment broadly.

• SoftBank's swings illustrate how concentrated AI bets amplify volatility across Asian markets.

• The interplay of yen, yields and AI makes Tokyo a key gauge of global risk appetite.

title: Gold Suffers Worst Week Since June as Rate-Hike Bets Bite
content: Spot gold ended Friday around $3,885 an ounce, nudging up on the day but down about 4.6% on the week — its steepest weekly fall since early June — after tumbling to a 52-week low near $3,853 on Thursday. The slide followed a hawkish repricing of Fed policy, with hot US inflation data and rising real yields denting the appeal of the non-yielding metal. Gold had traded above $4,050 only a week earlier, underscoring how quickly the rate outlook has shifted against it.
summary: Spot gold fell about 4.6% on the week, its worst since June, as rising US rate-hike bets and real yields hit the metal.
context:
• Gold had surged for much of 2026 on rate-cut hopes and safe-haven demand, pushing to records earlier in the year.

• The metal pays no income, so higher real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding it.

• A sharp shift from expected Fed cuts to possible hikes has reversed one of gold's main tailwinds.
happened:
• Spot gold closed Friday near $3,885 an ounce, up slightly on the day but down about 4.6% on the week.

• Prices hit a 52-week low around $3,853 on Thursday, having traded above $4,050 a week earlier.

• The drop coincided with firmer US inflation data, a stronger dollar and rising Treasury yields.
implications:
• Further hawkish Fed signals could keep pressure on gold and other precious metals into December.

• A deepening equity sell-off might yet revive safe-haven demand and cushion the decline.

• Sustained dollar strength would remain a headwind for dollar-priced commodities broadly.
importance:
• Gold's reversal is a clear read on how sharply rate expectations have repriced.

• The metal's slide alongside bonds and crypto shows the hawkish shock hitting multiple asset classes at once.

• Precious metals remain a key barometer of real yields and the inflation-policy balance.

title: Dollar Climbs to 19-Month High as Rate-Cut Bets Evaporate
content: The US dollar index rose to around 102.3 by mid-week, its strongest level since April 2025, as hotter-than-expected inflation and hawkish Fed commentary drove traders to abandon bets on near-term rate cuts. The greenback gained against every major currency, with the Australian dollar the weakest, off about 0.8%, followed by the Swiss franc and sterling, while the yen slipped roughly 0.6% and the euro eased about 0.5%. The move reflected a wholesale repricing of Fed expectations rather than a sudden burst of US growth.
summary: The dollar index hit its highest since April 2025 near 102.3 as hot inflation and hawkish Fed signals erased rate-cut bets.
context:
• The dollar's rally has been driven chiefly by shifting rate differentials as the Fed turns more hawkish than its peers.

• The euro, yen and sterling together dominate the dollar index, so their weakness mechanically lifts it.

• Other central banks, including the Bank of England at 4%, are seen on gentler paths, widening the gap with a firmer Fed.
happened:
• The dollar index climbed to about 102.3, its highest since April 2025, with the 10-year Treasury yield pushing near 4.99%.

• The greenback rose against all major peers; the Australian dollar fell about 0.8% and the yen around 0.6%.

• Analysts attributed the move to a repricing of Fed policy after firm US inflation data rather than stronger growth.
implications:
• A stronger dollar tightens global financial conditions and pressures emerging-market currencies and commodities.

• Persistent yen weakness raises the risk of Japanese official intervention and complicates Bank of Japan policy.

• Further hawkish surprises could extend the dollar's run into the December Fed meeting.
importance:
• The dollar is the linchpin of global finance, so its direction shapes capital flows worldwide.

• Its climb confirms that the hawkish Fed repricing is reverberating across currencies.

• Dollar strength is a key channel through which US rate shifts are exported to the rest of the world.
